tcas/0/p0.context: System note 'TCAS: Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System', section 'What it does — and what it doesn't', paragraph
tcas/0/p0.text: The TCAS described in the basic S-92 RFM alerts the crew with Traffic Advisories (TAs). It detects and tracks nearby transponder-equipped aircraft (ATCRBS Mode A/C or Mode S), computing range, relative bearing, closure rate, and — if the intruder reports it — relative altitude and vertical trend, to predict time to and separation at Closest Point of Approach (CPA). A TA fires when time to CPA is 15 to 30 seconds, alerting the crew with a 'Traffic, Traffic' aural and a TRAFFIC annunciation on the ADI.
tcas/0/p0.note: TCAS p.I-6-5 (DOC 450): ATCRBS (Mode A with/without C) or Mode S; range, bearing, closing rate, altitude if reporting; CPA; TA aural 'Traffic, Traffic' and TRAFFIC on the ADI; TA when time to CPA is 15 to 30 seconds. weather-radar/0/p0.context: System note 'Primus 700A Weather Radar', section 'What it is', paragraph
weather-radar/0/p0.text: The Honeywell Primus 700A is an X-band digital radar providing weather detection and high-resolution ground mapping, detecting storms within 60° of the flight path and displaying them on the MFDs. weather-radar/3/p0.context: System note 'Primus 700A Weather Radar', section 'Gain and tilt', paragraph
weather-radar/3/p0.text: Gain is normally automatic — Sensitivity Time Control (STC) compensates for signal weakening with distance, and REACT (when active) further adjusts sensitivity to compensate for attenuation through weather. GAIN can be pulled out for manual control: clockwise from MIN increases gain to maximum at the 12 o'clock position, then continuing clockwise progressively reduces STC compensation toward MAX.

weather-radar/3/p1.context: System note 'Primus 700A Weather Radar', section 'Gain and tilt', paragraph
weather-radar/3/p1.text: TILT selects manual or automatic (autotilt) antenna tilt. In manual mode (TILT pushed in), tilt varies ±15° with the first ±5° expanded for precision; stabilization, if enabled, still functions in manual tilt. In autotilt (TILT pulled out), the antenna automatically sets the optimum tilt for altitude and range, trimmable ±2° — but autotilt cannot compensate for high ground, and at long ranges (200–300 NM) earth curvature will put ground targets in the center of the display regardless.

egpws/0/p0.context: System note 'EGPWS', section 'What it is', paragraph
egpws/0/p0.text: EGPWS reduces Controlled Flight Into Terrain (CFIT) risk through two complementary alert families: the basic modes (2 through 6), based on radar altitude, which prevent descent into level or evenly sloping terrain; and the Look-Ahead modes, based on GPS position compared against terrain and obstacle databases, which catch sharply rising terrain or man-made obstacles ahead of the flight path.
egpws/0/p0.note: EGPWS Introduction p.I-4-35 (DOC 391): basic modes 2 through 6 on radar altitude, prevent descent into level or evenly sloping terrain; look ahead on GPS vs terrain/obstacle databases for sharply rising terrain or man made obstacles. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

egpws/0/p1.context: System note 'EGPWS', section 'What it is', paragraph

egpws/0/p1.note: p.I-4-37 (DOC 393) Basic Modes: mode 1 (high descent rate) is not used in the S-92. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

egpws/0/p2.context: System note 'EGPWS', section 'What it is', paragraph
egpws/0/p2.text: A geometric altitude — barometric altitude, radar altitude, and GPS altitude combined — drives the terrain display and alerting, preventing errors from a wrong altimeter setting, a faulty altimeter, or extreme cold. The obstacle database covers man-made structures over 100 ft high; not all obstacles are covered worldwide, and power lines are generally not included.
egpws/0/p2.note: p.I-4-35 (DOC 391): barometric, radar and GPS altitude combined into geometric altitude, prevents errors from wrong altimeter setting, faulty altimeter or extreme cold; obstacle database more than 100 feet; not all obstacles, some areas no coverage; power lines generally not included. egpws/2/p0.text: Using the predicted flight path vector compared to the terrain/obstacle database, Look-Ahead issues a caution at roughly 30 seconds from impact and escalates to a warning at roughly 20 seconds — both remain active until the aircraft maneuvers clear. Alert timing is slightly reduced in low altitude mode.

egpws/2/p1.text: Look-Ahead is inhibited when TER INHB is selected or airspeed is below 70 KIAS. If GPS is lost, EGPWS dead-reckons for 60 seconds; if GPS isn't regained, a 'BE ALERT, TERRAIN INOP' aural sounds and the terrain map is removed.

egpws/2/p2.text: When an alert occurs, the terrain display range automatically changes to 5 NM (2.5 NM in low altitude mode) and the offending terrain area is enlarged on the display (cell expansion) to draw attention to it. If no terrain display is selected anywhere when an alert triggers, the system pops one up automatically — center MFD first, then pilot inboard, then copilot inboard MFD (disabled with two or fewer MFDs operational).

afcs/0/p1.context: System note 'AFCS: The Coupled Flight Director', section 'The architecture', paragraph
afcs/0/p1.text: Three layers stack on top of each other. SAS provides basic rate damping — it senses a disturbance (a gust-induced nose pitch-up, say) and makes small, immediate corrections without trying to return the aircraft to its original attitude. AP adds attitude hold on top of SAS: it remembers the trimmed pitch/roll/yaw attitude and actively works to regain it after a disturbance, plus hover augmentation, gust alleviation, and heading hold (below 50 KIAS) or heading hold with turn coordination (above 50 KIAS). The Coupled Flight Director (CFD) sits on top of both, using the trim actuators to fly a pilot-selected path hands-off.

Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

afcs/1/p0.context: System note 'AFCS: The Coupled Flight Director', section 'SAS servos vs. trim actuators — what actually moves the stick', paragraph
afcs/1/p0.text: Two sets of four hydraulic SAS servos (eight total, two per axis) make control inputs without moving the cockpit controls — each servo has 5% control authority, combining to 10% total per axis. If a primary SAS computer or its sensors fail, the pilot can select secondary SAS, in which the AP computer (using AHRS data) takes over that side.
afcs/1/p0.note: p.I-16-3 (DOC 510): two sets of four hydraulic SAS servos (eight), two per axis, 5% each, 10% total; controls do not move; secondary SAS: AP computer using AHRS controls that side. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

afcs/1/p1.context: System note 'AFCS: The Coupled Flight Director', section 'SAS servos vs. trim actuators — what actually moves the stick', paragraph
afcs/1/p1.text: Four electromechanical trim actuators, by contrast, do move the cockpit controls when they move — they provide control referencing and an artificial control gradient, each with 100% control authority but limited to 10%/second rate. Once trimmed, any control movement without releasing trim builds an increasing force back toward the reference. Trim actuators are what the AP and CFD use for their control inputs.

afcs/4/p0.context: System note 'AFCS: The Coupled Flight Director', section 'Power limiting', paragraph
afcs/4/p0.text: When coupled to the collective axis, the CFD automatically limits power to maximum continuous torque/TGT/Ng. On a power limit, the CFD trades airspeed to hold the desired altitude or climb rate, working toward bucket airspeed (minimum power required speed — 80 KIAS at sea level, decreasing 1 kt per 1,000 ft). If the aircraft reaches bucket speed and still can't hold the target, it will instead descend (in ALT) or reduce climb rate (in VS), with a yellow CHECK POWER advisory and a single aural alert.

afcs/5/p0.context: System note 'AFCS: The Coupled Flight Director', section 'Engine failure while coupled', paragraph
afcs/5/p0.text: The pilot should always take manual control and fly the appropriate emergency procedure — but the CFD's automatic behavior in the interim is worth knowing. Coupled to the collective (three-cue): the CFD automatically lowers collective to restore Nr to 105% and stay below maximum continuous power, resetting the airspeed reference to bucket speed. Coupled to altitude/VS on the pitch axis (two-cue): the aircraft tries to hold by reducing airspeed; if power still isn't sufficient and airspeed drops below 50 KIAS, it auto-decouples — take control before decelerating below bucket speed. Airspeed coupled to pitch with no vertical mode selected: the airspeed reference resets to bucket speed automatically. If both engines fail while coupled, the collective axis auto-decouples.

afcs/6/p1.context: System note 'AFCS: The Coupled Flight Director', section 'Approach modes', paragraph
afcs/6/p1.text: On an ILS with GS and DCL armed, the CFD flies a pre-programmed deceleration to 80 KIAS by 200 ft AGL, continuing to 60 KIAS by 50 ft AGL, leveling at 50 ft AGL if GS is selected — the radar altimeter must be valid for DCL to function, and changing the airspeed reference while DCL is armed will de-arm it. P-ILS lets the CFD carry ILS-style glideslope, deceleration, and level-off features on an FMS-based approach, transitioning automatically from FMS flight plan to FMS approach to P-ILS as each phase is intercepted.

electrical-power-system/0/p0.context: System note 'Electrical Power System', section 'The AC side', paragraph
electrical-power-system/0/p0.text: Two oil-cooled brushless main generators produce three-phase 115 VAC at 420 Hz, driven off the main transmission accessory modules. They are rated 75 kVA continuous and 90 kVA transient. Each has its own Generator Control Unit in the cabin overhead that regulates output and protects against over- and under-voltage, feeder fault, and under-frequency — the under-frequency protection is disabled when the helicopter is off the ground (weight-off-wheels).

electrical-power-system/2/p0.context: System note 'Electrical Power System', section 'The DC side, and how it heals itself', paragraph
electrical-power-system/2/p0.text: Two AC-powered 400-amp DC converters make 28 VDC for the two primary DC buses, the DC essential bus, and the battery, battery hold-up, and battery utility buses. electrical-power-system/5/p1.context: System note 'Electrical Power System', section 'Why this matters for the landing gear', paragraph
electrical-power-system/5/p1.text: Cushioning a single-engine landing, Nr can droop below 96% and drop both AC generators offline at touchdown. Unless the APU is on with its generator switch on, only the battery bus is left powering the aircraft and the copilot MFDs blank momentarily. Control is unaffected, and normal supply returns once collective is lowered and Nr recovers above 96%.

fuel-system/0/p0.context: System note 'Fuel System', section 'What it is', paragraph
fuel-system/0/p0.text: A separate suction fuel system for each engine. Fuel is held in two crash-resistant nylon-reinforced rubber bladder tanks, one in each sponson, roughly 382 US gallons each. The No. 1 tank feeds the No. 1 engine and the APU; the No. 2 tank feeds the No. 2 engine. A single-point pressure refuel/defuel fitting is on the left side, and both tanks can also be gravity refuelled.

fuel-system/0/p1.text: Fuel capacity is 713 US gallons, about 2,190 kg (4,830 lb) of Jet A/JP-8, on a gravity fill and 764 US gallons, about 2,345 kg (5,175 lb), on a pressure fill (standard-day weights). Of that, 4.8 gallons is unusable — 2.4 gallons in each tank.

fuel-system/1/p0.context: System note 'Fuel System', section 'The fuel control switches', paragraph
fuel-system/1/p0.text: One switch per tank on the engine control quadrant, marked NO. 1 FUEL and NO. 2 FUEL, with positions OFF, XFD, and DIRECT. OFF closes the fuel control valve and shuts fuel off to that engine — this is also the engine-fire and engine-shutdown selection. DIRECT opens the valve so the engine draws from its own-side tank. XFD feeds that engine from the opposite tank; a check valve in each crossfeed line stops air from a dead engine's line reaching the running engine.

fuel-system/2/note.context: System note 'Fuel System', section 'Crossfeed limits', table note
fuel-system/2/note.text: On extended single-engine flight, crossfeed is used to keep the tank imbalance under 317 kg (700 lb) or to stop the good engine starving — but not if a fuel-system malfunction is suspected as the cause of the failure. An imbalance over 317 kg (700 lb) combined with grossly unbalanced cabin loading can put the aircraft outside lateral CG limits.

fuel-system/3/p0.context: System note 'Fuel System', section 'Prime pumps', paragraph
fuel-system/3/p0.text: Two electric prime pumps in the left cabin sidewall, controlled by the FUEL PRIME switch with AUTO, PUMP 1, and PUMP 2 positions. Only one runs at a time; in AUTO the active pump alternates on successive uses, switching with each MDC power cycle. They deliver pressurised fuel for engine start when the fuel switch is in DIRECT; started in XFD, the prime fuel goes to the opposite engine.

fuel-system/4/p0.context: System note 'Fuel System', section 'Prime shutoff valves', paragraph
fuel-system/4/p0.text: Each prime shutoff valve is position-monitored, and a mismatch between commanded and actual position posts SOV1 WRNG POSN or SOV2 WRNG POSN. There are two failure modes: stuck open when commanded closed, and stuck closed when commanded open — a valve stuck closed makes that engine start very slowly. In flight the response is to continue and correct before the next flight.

fuel-system/5/p0.text: Each tank has two quantity probes at front and rear for an attitude-compensated level, a low-level sensor, and two high-level sensors, all feeding a common Fuel Conditioning Unit that sends quantity to the EICAS pages; fuel flow comes from each engine's FADEC. FUEL 1 LOW or FUEL 2 LOW appears at roughly 98 ± 20 kg (215 ± 45 lb) remaining in that tank and turns the EICAS fuel figure yellow. With a LOW caution lit, steady pitch attitudes over 10° nose-up or below 5° nose-down are avoided to prevent unporting, and the procedure is to land as soon as practical.

auxiliary-power-unit/0/p0.context: System note 'Auxiliary Power Unit', section 'What it is', paragraph
auxiliary-power-unit/0/p0.text: A GTCP36-150 APU, mounted behind and to the right of the No. 1 engine, with its intake on the rear of the main rotor pylon and its exhaust behind and below the No. 1 engine exhaust. It supplies electrical power on the ground with the rotors stopped, emergency electrical power in flight, bleed air for engine starting, and bleed heat for the cockpit and cabin. Its fuel comes from the No. 1 tank. Maximum airspeed with the APU operating is 150 KIAS.

auxiliary-power-unit/1/p0.context: System note 'Auxiliary Power Unit', section 'Hydraulic start, not electric', paragraph
auxiliary-power-unit/1/p0.text: The APU starter is a hydraulic motor. Its energy is stored in an accumulator in the cabin overhead — a piston separating nitrogen at 2,500 to 4,000 psig from hydraulic fluid. The No. 3 hydraulic system recharges it, and a hand pump in the overhead is the manual backup when No. 3 pressure is unavailable. The gauge reads 4,000 psig fully charged and 2,500 psig discharged, and APU ACCUM LOW illuminates at 3,450 psig. A start can be re-attempted once the ACCUM LOW advisory goes out.

auxiliary-power-unit/2/p0.context: System note 'Auxiliary Power Unit', section 'The start sequence', paragraph
auxiliary-power-unit/2/p0.text: APU CTRL to ON gives a four-second BIT delay, then the Electronic Sequencing Unit runs the start: prime pump on, APU start valve open to route accumulator pressure through the starter motor, igniter on. At 10% speed the fuel shutoff solenoid and ignition energise; at 50% the start valve closes and the starter is secured; at 94.5% the ignition unit is secured and the hour meter and start counter begin. The APU ON advisory confirms it is running.

mgb-lubrication-warning-system/0/p0.context: System note 'MGB Lubrication and Warning System', section 'What it is', paragraph
mgb-lubrication-warning-system/0/p0.text: The Main Gearbox (MGB) sits atop the cabin forward of the two engines, built from five modules — two input modules, two accessory modules, and the main module — with a built-in 5° forward tilt. Dual pumps mounted on the front of the MGB supply cooled, filtered oil to all bearings and gears; an external radiator cooled by a blower on the tail rotor drive shaft prevents overheating, with a bypass valve able to isolate the cooler entirely. The oil filter has an impending-bypass button that should be checked on preflight for contamination.

mgb-lubrication-warning-system/4/p0.context: System note 'MGB Lubrication and Warning System', section 'Chip detection', paragraph
mgb-lubrication-warning-system/4/p0.text: Five chip detectors — one each in the MGB, both input modules, and both accessory modules — feed a chip detector processor, generating MGB CHIP, INPUT 1/2 CHIP, and ACC 1/2 CHIP cautions independently. A 30-second time-delay relay lets small chips and fuzz burn off or wash away before triggering a caution, preventing false alarms from normal wear debris — this fuzz burn-off function is what MGB OIL HOT disables. The detector runs a Built-In-Test on startup; a BIT failure shows CHIP SYS FAULT.

Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

mgb-lubrication-warning-system/5/p0.context: System note 'MGB Lubrication and Warning System', section 'Bearing Monitor System (BMS)', paragraph
mgb-lubrication-warning-system/5/p0.text: The BMS processes vibration and temperature data from the swashplate, tail rotor drive shaft bearings #1 and #2, and the oil cooler bearing. An out-of-limit reading on any of them illuminates CHECK BMS. Swashplate over-temperature specifically can escalate to a warning or caution depending on severity — a separate, more serious condition from the routine BMS advisory.
mgb-lubrication-warning-system/5/p0.note: p.I-12-3 (DOC 489) BMS: swashplate, tail rotor drive shaft bearings #1 and #2, oil cooler bearing; CHECK BMS advisory; warning or caution if swashplate temperature rises above normal. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

mgb-lubrication-warning-system/6/p0.context: System note 'MGB Lubrication and Warning System', section 'Rotor brake — a separate hydraulic circuit', paragraph
mgb-lubrication-warning-system/6/p0.text: The rotor brake pad/disc assembly mounts on the MGB tail rotor output flange, engaged by pulling down and forward on a handle over the pilot's left shoulder — more forward movement or repeated strokes increases brake pressure, shown on an adjacent gauge. The rotor brake reservoir doubles as the servicing reservoir for hydraulic systems 1, 2, and 3.

Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

mgb-lubrication-warning-system/6/p1.context: System note 'MGB Lubrication and Warning System', section 'Rotor brake — a separate hydraulic circuit', paragraph
mgb-lubrication-warning-system/6/p1.text: Both engines can be started with the rotor brake set — the FADEC won't advance either engine past idle until Np exceeds 24%. The rotor brake holds the rotor stationary during engine start and slows or stops it after engine shutdown — it is not designed to stop the rotor before the engines are shut down. Pressure and puck-position sensors drive the ROTOR BRAKE caution: on the ground, either sensor alone triggers it; in the air, both sensors must agree to trigger it.

hydraulic-system/0/p0.context: System note 'Hydraulic System', section 'Three independent systems, full redundancy', paragraph
hydraulic-system/0/p0.text: No. 1 and No. 2 are the primary flight-control hydraulic systems, each fully capable on its own. No. 3 is a genuine backup — it can supply either or both of No. 1/No. 2 if a pump fails, and independently powers the landing gear, cargo ramp, and automatic APU accumulator recharge. All three are completely independent. The No. 1 and No. 2 pumps are constant-pressure (4,000 psi) with a variable flow of up to 13 GPM; their pump modules are identical and interchangeable, driven by their respective accessory modules. No. 3 is driven directly off the main gearbox, with a separate reservoir and an AC-motor-driven ground-checkout mode for pre-rotor testing.
hydraulic-system/0/p0.note: HYDRAULIC SYSTEM p.I-14-1 (DOC 500): No. 1/2 full pressure for flight controls; No. 3 backup to either/both, landing gear, ramp, APU accumulator recharge; completely independent; p.I-14-2 (DOC 501): No. 1/2 constant pressure 4000 psi, variable flow up to 13 GPM, identical and interchangeable, driven by accessory modules; No. 3 driven by MGB, separate reservoir, AC motor for ground operation. FIXED 2026-09-26: attributed 4000 psi constant pressure to all three systems; the RFM gives it for No. 1 and No. 2. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

hydraulic-system/0/p1.context: System note 'Hydraulic System', section 'Three independent systems, full redundancy', paragraph
hydraulic-system/0/p1.text: A four-channel boost system (collective, pitch, roll, yaw) is powered by No. 2 hydraulics via a BST switch — turning it OFF illuminates BOOST PRES and noticeably increases control forces (cyclic roughly 0.5 kg → 2.7 kg / 1 lb → 6 lb per axis; collective/yaw roughly 1.8 kg → 5.9 kg / 4 lb → 13 lb), with some collective-to-yaw interaction. SAS hydraulic power comes through shutoff valves on the pilot-assist manifold, controlled by the SAS1/SAS2 switches on the AFCS panel — below 1,100 psi, SAS 1 PRES or SAS 2 PRES illuminates.
hydraulic-system/0/p1.note: p.I-14-1 (DOC 500): four channel boost, No. 2 hydraulics, BST switch; OFF gives BOOST PRES; cyclic 1 to 6 lb each axis, collective and yaw 4 to 13 lb; collective to yaw interaction; SAS1/SAS2 shutoff valves on pilot assist manifold; below 1100 psi SAS 1/2 PRES. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

hydraulic-system/1/p0.context: System note 'Hydraulic System', section 'The SERVO switch — isolating one side deliberately', paragraph
hydraulic-system/1/p0.text: A SERVO switch (NO. 1 / BOTH / NO. 2) on the upper console turns off one side of the three primary flight-control servos and the tail rotor servo. Selecting NO. 1 turns off the No. 2 servo side (MR SVO 2 PRES and TR SVO 2 PRES illuminate); selecting NO. 2 turns off the No. 1 side (MR SVO 1 PRES and TR SVO 1 PRES illuminate). An interlock prevents deliberately turning off a servo side while the other side has already lost pressure — and if the side left running loses pressure, the previously-off side automatically re-enables.

Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

hydraulic-system/2/p0.context: System note 'Hydraulic System', section 'Automatic backup shutoff valves', paragraph
hydraulic-system/2/p0.text: Both backup shutoff valves (which connect No. 3 to No. 1/No. 2) close automatically during engine start and shutdown, to prevent unwanted pressure shuttling between systems. During start, the DCUs close them once the first engine passes 15% Ng, reopening once Nr exceeds 50%. During shutdown, they close once Nr drops below 50%, reopening two minutes after the last engine's Ng drops below 15%.
hydraulic-system/2/p0.note: p.I-14-3/I-14-4 (DOC 502-503): backup shutoff valves close during start and shutdown; start: close when first engine above 15% Ng, reopen above 50% Nr; shutdown: close below 50% Nr, reopen two minutes after last engine Ng below 15%. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

hydraulic-system/2/p1.context: System note 'Hydraulic System', section 'Automatic backup shutoff valves', paragraph
hydraulic-system/2/p1.text: With the backup shutoff valves closed, No. 3 pressure is unavailable to the primary, SAS, and boost servos — but remains available for the ramp, landing gear, and APU accumulator. During engine start, the pilot cannot move the flight controls until No. 1 and/or No. 2 pressure is established, regardless of No. 3 status; after shutdown, No. 3 can't be used to move the flight controls until the two-minute reopen delay has elapsed.
hydraulic-system/2/p1.note: p.I-14-4 (DOC 503): valves closed: No. 3 not to primary, SAS or boost servos; available for ramp, APU accumulator and landing gear; NOTE controls cannot be moved during start until system 1 and/or 2 pressure; after shutdown not with system 3 until two minutes. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

hydraulic-system/3/p0.context: System note 'Hydraulic System', section 'Leak Detection and Isolation (LDI)', paragraph
hydraulic-system/3/p0.text: If a No. 1 or No. 2 reservoir level drops below its set limit: the corresponding RSVR LOW caution illuminates, that system's tail rotor shutoff valve closes to isolate a possible leak in the tail rotor circuit, and its backup shutoff valve closes to isolate the leaking primary system from No. 3 — protecting the No. 3 backup capability for the still-healthy system. A subsequent leak in the other primary system does not also trigger those valves; each side is isolated independently as its own leak is detected.
hydraulic-system/3/p0.note: p.I-14-4 (DOC 503) LDI: No. 1 or No. 2 reservoir below set limit: RSVR LOW, tail rotor shutoff valve closes, backup shutoff valve closes; subsequent leak in other primary system will not cause those valves to close. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

engine-blowaway-oei-power/0/p0.context: System note 'Engine: Blowaway Logic and OEI Power', section 'What it is', paragraph
engine-blowaway-oei-power/0/p0.text: Two CT7-8/CT7-8A turboshaft engines, each controlled by a dual-channel FADEC (channels A and B swap control after every shutdown; a degraded channel hands control to the healthier one). During normal all-engines-operative flight, the FADEC holds Nr at a constant 105% with matched torque between engines — though if a high-margin engine is paired with a low-margin one, the FADEC will command up to a 10% torque split at the upper power ranges to compensate.

engine-blowaway-oei-power/1/p0.context: System note 'Engine: Blowaway Logic and OEI Power', section 'How blowaway triggers', paragraph
engine-blowaway-oei-power/1/p0.text: When the AEO takeoff limit is reached (100% torque or 995°C TGT), the FADEC limits fuel flow, causing Nr to droop. If that droop takes Nr below 100%, blowaway activates: if both engines are on a TGT limit, the FADEC automatically shifts them into the 30-second power TGT rating (no TGT blowaway exists for OEI). If the aircraft is limited by MGB torque instead, the FADEC increases the torque limit per the blowaway schedule — separate schedules exist for dual-engine and single-engine conditions, and for normal vs. training modes.

engine-blowaway-oei-power/4/p1.context: System note 'Engine: Blowaway Logic and OEI Power', section 'How each OEI range gets armed', paragraph
engine-blowaway-oei-power/4/p1.text: The pilot can also select manually via the OEI SEL switch: push forward for 30-second power, pull back for two-minute power, plunge down for maximum continuous. rotor-ice-protection-system/0/p0.context: System note 'Rotor Ice Protection System (RIPS)', section 'What it is', paragraph
rotor-ice-protection-system/0/p0.text: Electrothermal de-icing for the main and tail rotor blades, certified for icing conditions up to 10,000 ft pressure altitude. It must be ON for any flight into icing; flight in freezing drizzle, freezing rain, or supercooled large drops is prohibited regardless. Power-up checks can run on any single AC source — either main generator, the APU generator, or external power — but normal blade heating needs power from at least one main generator, so on APU-only power the blade elements are load-shed.
rotor-ice-protection-system/0/p0.note: RIPS p.I-18-22 (DOC 550): deicing up to 10,000 feet; power-up checks on any AC source (#1/#2 generator, APU generator, external); blade elements require at least one main generator; p.1-5 (DOC 31): RIPS on for icing; freezing drizzle/rain/SLD prohibited; p.I-2-7 (DOC 345): blade de-ice load-shed on APU generator. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

rotor-ice-protection-system/1/p0.context: System note 'Rotor Ice Protection System (RIPS)', section 'The heating elements', paragraph
rotor-ice-protection-system/1/p0.text: Each main rotor blade carries four spanwise electrothermal elements bonded into the leading edge beneath the nickel/titanium abrasion strip. Element pairs on opposite blades form one zone, so the 16 main rotor elements make eight zones, heated sequentially blade-pair by blade-pair so accreted ice sheds symmetrically. The four tail rotor blades have one spanwise element each, energised all together. Each main rotor droop-stop shaft is heated continuously whenever RIPS is on and OAT is below +5°C, until landing or OAT rises back above +5°C.
rotor-ice-protection-system/1/p0.note: p.I-18-22 (DOC 550): four spanwise elements per main blade beneath nickel/titanium strip; opposite pairs form zones, sixteen elements eight zones, sequential, symmetric shedding; tail rotor one element per blade, all four simultaneously; p.I-18-25 (DOC 553): droop stop heaters when OAT less than +5°C and RIPS on, until landing or OAT above +5°C. Checked on the rendered page image 2026-09-26.

rotor-ice-protection-system/2/p0.context: System note 'Rotor Ice Protection System (RIPS)', section 'Dual everything', paragraph
rotor-ice-protection-system/2/p0.text: Two RIPS controllers in the cabin ceiling, each able to run the system alone: one is master, the other is slave monitoring it, and they swap on a failure or a reset. The main rotor distributor on the head (fed through a slip ring), the junction box, and the slip ring assembly each have two channels. The main rotor slip ring rides on a duplex bearing with its own monitor — a SLIPRING BRNG advisory means the primary bearing has failed and the secondary allows about 10 more hours.
rotor-ice-protection-system/2/p0.note: p.I-18-24 (DOC 552): two RIPS controllers in the cabin ceiling, each can operate alone; master/slave; swap on failure or on power application/reset; p.I-18-22 (DOC 550): distributor and junction box two channels; slip ring redundant; duplex bearing and monitor; SLIPRING BRNG, secondary bearing another 10 hours. rotor-ice-protection-system/3/p1.context: System note 'Rotor Ice Protection System (RIPS)', section 'How AUTO schedules heat', paragraph
rotor-ice-protection-system/3/p1.text: Lose all LWC input and AUTO reverts to an OFF schedule for a default 0.35 g/m³, equivalent to mid-LIGHT icing; lose OAT input and it uses a default −12°C for the ON schedule. An OAT interlock blocks blade heating above +5°C, and a weight-on-wheels interlock blocks it on the ground.

rotor-ice-protection-system/5/p1.context: System note 'Rotor Ice Protection System (RIPS)', section 'Ground override, tests, and reset', paragraph
rotor-ice-protection-system/5/p1.text: PBIT runs on power-up (everything except the heating elements), CBIT runs continuously, and IBIT is pilot-initiated from the system status page — about 30 to 90 seconds during which RIPS is inoperative and a TEST icon shows below the ice-rate meter; the IBIT is completed before the first icing flight of the day. A reset is holding BLADE DEICE #1 RESET and #2 RESET on the copilot overhead for about 3 seconds until the ICE icon replaces the ice-rate meter; it briefly removes power and swaps the master controller. A reset is the first action for most RIPS cautions — DEICE SYS FAIL, MR DEICE FAULT, MR DEICE FAIL, AUTO DEICE FAIL, TR DEICE FAIL — and the rotor keeps accreting ice through the 30-to-90-second reset.

rotor-ice-protection-system/6/p0.context: System note 'Rotor Ice Protection System (RIPS)', section 'Vibration is the cue', paragraph
rotor-ice-protection-system/6/p0.text: In normal operation airframe vibration and power required both cycle as the blades accrete and shed — up to roughly 15% torque change, more at high altitude and gross weight, which shows up as reduced all-engines climb capability. Cyclic swings are expected. Steadily increasing, as opposed to cyclic, vibration or power required may indicate run-back ice; if it keeps increasing with a degraded RIPS, the response is to exit icing and avoid further flight in icing. A DROOP HTR FAIL caution risks a hung droop stop on the next rotor shutdown.

emergency-flotation-system/0/p0.context: System note 'Emergency Flotation System', section 'What it's designed to do', paragraph
emergency-flotation-system/0/p0.text: At aircraft weights at or above 8,432 kg (18,590 lb), the system is designed to keep the helicopter upright and afloat long enough for full evacuation in mid Sea State 5 (8–12 ft waves, 18–25 kt wind). Below that weight, the design margin is mid Sea State 4 (4–8 ft waves, 17–21 kt wind).
